source.title: Revisiting the Shape Convention of Transformer Language Models
source.authors: FengTing Liao; G. Yi; Tzu-Quan Lin; Meng-Hsi Chen; Da-Shan Shiu

record.tranche_reason: The study trains and evaluates Transformer variants with different FFN shapes, widths, depths and attention dimensions, including matched-parameter comparisons. This conceptually tests V4, but it does not fit or test the claimed scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether architectural shape changes held-out language-model loss, chiefly through controlled and parameter-matched comparisons. It does not test power-law scaling, small-run extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or downstream predictability. Prior scaling-law results in the background are cited rather than newly tested.
record.test_reason: The study trains parameter-matched Transformers that differ in FFN shape, width, depth and attention width, and compares held-out validation loss. This is a different method aimed at V4's question: does shape at fixed parameter count change loss much? It fits no power law, extrapolation or compute-optimal split. Its one log-linear fit of downstream accuracy against compute bears weakly on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the narrow-wide-narrow FFN is not essential: parameter-matched Hourglass Transformers (113M–8B) match conventional validation and downstream quality while allowing wider, shallower models. The paraphrase omits several claimed benefits: 8.7% less training compute at matched downstream accuracy, better post-YaRN long-context results, and up to 1.93× faster 64k decoding. The authors also stress that large-scale results validate the joint recipe, not each factor separately.
record.recipe_differences: The original sources fit loss scaling laws and compute-optimal allocations; this study compares trained architectures and measures validation quality under shape changes rather than fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with FFN ratio and depth, model configuration, attention dimension, and context-extension setting. The paper reports a quality–compute trade-off across the hourglass design space.
record.problems: The authors state that large-scale experiments jointly vary FFN shape, residual width, layer count and attention projection width, so they do not isolate each factor at every scale. The comprehensive parameter search is constrained to smaller scales; the recipe is validated up to 8B and 160B tokens. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the 16 per-dataset validation-loss entries in Table 6 (906M and 3B, four datasets, two architectures) to stay within the 60-row limit after retaining aggregate validation results and the distinct long-context comparison. Also omitted downstream accuracy and RULER accuracy because they are not validation loss measures for V4.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Only three paired scales (906M, 3B, 8B) are reported, without a fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No compute-optimal sweep; token counts are fixed at the Chinchilla ratio of about 20 tokens per parameter.
No other modality or regime scaling. YaRN extension is not a scaling-law test.
Downstream predictability is tested only through a 3-point log-linear fit per architecture; there is no fit of downstream performance on pretraining loss.
No study of fitting choices or curvature.
Large-scale comparisons vary FFN shape, width, depth and attention width jointly. Aspect ratios are tested only up to 8B and 160B tokens. Most points use a single seed with no uncertainty.

missing.what: Log-linear fits of average downstream accuracy on total training compute (R² = 0.996 and 0.997), plus the derived 8.7% compute saving at matched accuracy
906M Hourglass width/depth sweep: validation PPL delta vs d_model/L for L∈{12,16} and several d_h/d_model, all within about ±1% of baseline at matched parameters
403M Hourglass d_h/d_model sweep at (K,L)=(4,12) and (4,24), competitive with or below the conventional baseline PPL at matched parameters
Per-dataset validation loss for 906M and 3B; differences ≤0.024 loss on every dataset (largest on M2D2 at 3B)

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's partial state on the reduced-depth rows is changed to observed: a 1.1% loss change is the small effect V4 predicts. The attention-dimension rows change parameter count, so they are unlinked from V4. Table 10/11 ablations vary model size along with K or d_h, so they are not fixed-N shape tests and are correctly not rows. Most runs use a single seed and report no uncertainty, so gaps under 1% may be noise. The authors cite Kaplan et al. as finding hourglass FFNs underperform; this study extends V4's range to d_h < d_model.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction from smaller runs to larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or fitted growth exponents.
Tests a finite set of FFN, width, depth and attention configurations, not a broad or exhaustive range of architecture details.
No other modalities or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling-law tests; the YaRN context-extension evaluation is not a test of the same power-law claim.
Reports downstream task scores but does not test whether they improve predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
Does not study scaling-law fitting choices or whether fitted scaling curves bend.

relation.reason: The study reports its own architecture-shape comparisons and downstream accuracy-versus-compute fits.

tranche.reason: Controlled architecture comparisons at approximately fixed parameter budgets directly test V4 using held-out loss, rather than fitting the original scaling laws.

source_check.notes: Parameter counts exclude embeddings; budgets are approximately matched, and all experiments use one fixed seed. Long-context and pretraining comparisons use different evaluation corpora, so their gap difference does not isolate a training-stage effect.

statements.correction: Table 7 conventional/Hourglass losses: 906M 3.092/3.095; 3B 2.646/2.651; 8B 2.414/2.409. Maximum absolute relative difference approximately 0.21%. Large-scale comparisons jointly change architecture dimensions; code and conventional baseline controls are reported.
statements.problem: The loss comparison is correct to rounding, but 'at most 0.2%' is slightly too strict: the displayed 8B values imply approximately 0.207%.

statements.correction: 8B pretraining validation averages four datasets: PPL 13.37 conventional versus 13.31 Hourglass. After 400-step YaRN extension, Proof-pile PPL is 7.39/7.10 at 4k and 4.79/4.55 at 64k. No matched Proof-pile before/after comparison is reported.
statements.problem: The post-extension gap is larger than the pretraining-validation gap, but the evaluations also change corpus and context length; growth attributable to fine-tuning is not isolated.

statements.correction: Table 2: 8B Hourglass validation PPL advantage 0.45% on the four-dataset average. Table 3: after identical YaRN extension, Hourglass has lower Proof-pile PPL at every evaluated length. The evaluations do not isolate the effect of fine-tuning.
statements.problem: A larger gap is observed in the post-extension evaluation, but training-stage dependence cannot be separated from corpus and context changes.
